Text-Driven 3D Hand Motion Generation from Sign Language Data
Léore Bensabath
Affiliation:
LIGM, École des Ponts, IP Paris, Univ Gustave Eiffel, CNRS
Email:
leore.bensabath@enpc.frhttps://imagine.enpc.fr/leore.bensabath/HandMDM
Mathis Petrovich
Affiliation:
NVIDIA
Gül Varol
Affiliation:
Affiliation:
LIGM, École des Ponts, IP Paris, Univ Gustave Eiffel, CNRS
Abstract
Our goal is to train a generative model of 3D hand motions, conditioned on natural language descriptions specifying motion characteristics such as handshapes, locations, finger/hand/arm movements. To this end, we automatically build pairs of 3D hand motions and their associated textual labels with unprecedented scale. Specifically, we leverage a large-scale sign language video dataset, along with noisy pseudo-annotated sign categories, which we translate into hand motion descriptions via an LLM that utilizes a dictionary of sign attributes, as well as our complementary motion-script cues. This data enables training a text-conditioned hand motion diffusion model (HandMDM), that is robust across domains such as unseen sign categories from the same sign language, but also signs from another sign language and non-sign hand movements. We contribute extensive experimental investigation of these scenarios and will make our trained models and data publicly available to support future research in this relatively new field.
Figure 1
:
3D hand motion from text:
We collect BOBSL3DT, a dataset of hand motions with accompanying textual descriptions,
which we use to train a hand motion diffusion model (HandMDM).
We provide
example motion-text pairs from our dataset depicting rich handshapes and movements.
For dynamic visualizations, we refer to
Fig.
A.6
of the appendix
and the video on our project page.
1
Introduction
Human hand motion modeling is at the center of multiple research areas, ranging from
sign languages
[
88
,
11
]
or gestures accompanying speech
[
53
]
,
to object interactions
[
20
]
. In this paper, we explore the limits of
text control
for generating
3D hand motions, i.e., we ask the question whether open-vocabulary language descriptions
(such as
‘index and little fingers extended’
in
Fig.
1
)
can be used to drive a generative model of hands.
This is a relatively new task, with very recent interest in the context
of hand-object interaction
[
14
,
13
]
, and body-motion conditioning
[
91
]
.
Here, we consider text to be the only control signal for hands, and
study complex hand motions mainly in the context of sign language data.
Recent advances in text-conditioned
human
body motion
generation
have attracted a large interest
[
58
,
81
]
,
but one of the main limitations has been identified as the lack
of detailed
hand
movements to achieve expressiveness
[
38
]
.
The reason primarily stems from lack of data.
Commonly used motion capture datasets do not contain hand articulations
[
47
]
;
in return, corresponding textual annotations do not describe hands
[
26
,
63
,
61
]
.
There are a few exceptions with Motion-X
[
38
]
being one, where
they resort to video-based whole-body capture and
employ a rule-based script to
encode handshapes according to spatial relations among fingers, similar to
PoseScript
[
16
]
for static bodies. However, the overall database
remains still very body-focused, as also judged by the very recent work of
[
91
]
.
To collect hand-centric annotations,
[
91
]
manually annotated the BOTH57M dataset,
capturing 3.2k
full-body motions with detailed hands in a multi-camera studio setup.
Due to the prohibitively expensive process, the resulting dataset is relatively small.
The key challenge is how to scale up the number of
motions
and
labels
to train a robust model.
Our solution leverages several enabling factors:
(i) We turn to the BOBSL
[
2
]
dataset, comprising 1,400 hours of British Sign Language (BSL) videos, exhaustively pseudo-labeled with sign estimates
[
67
]
.
(ii) We employ state-of-the-art monocular reconstruction methods such as HAMER
[
57
]
for hands,
and SMPLer-X
[
9
]
for bodies to estimate accurate 3D upper body motions from these videos.
(iii) We exploit SignBank
[
21
]
, a dictionary of BSL signs, with 4k
glosses
1
1
1
Glosses are written words associated to individual signs (
see
Appendix
A
).
, each marked with several attributes denoting handshapes, initial/final hand locations, and other phonological information. (iv) We complement SignBank by detecting certain pose features from motions via rule-based scripts. (v) We provide all these information per gloss category to a large language model (LLM)
[
23
]
to turn them into natural language descriptions.
With the above ingredients, we transfer textual gloss descriptions from SignBank to BOBSL sign videos by matching
the pseudo-labels to glosses, resulting in our BOBSL3DT dataset consisting of
1.3M
motion-text pairs.
Note that there are several sources of noise, making it challenging to train a model on this data.
In particular, a given pseudo-label word may map to multiple sign variants in SignBank. Therefore, the transfer
of gloss descriptions to pseudo-labels is not straightforward, since we do not know a priori
which variant BOBSL sign corresponds to.
While we detail the exact process in
Sec.
3
, in simple terms, we estimate the variant performed in each BOBSL sign
by matching to its closest motion from SignBank videos.
Besides this assignment noise, the pseudo-labels themselves are not always correct, the 3D reconstructions may be imprecise,
and the LLM may not capture all the motion details.
Considering the noise-scale trade-off and following the trend in modern computer vision
[
66
,
49
]
, we go towards high-scale & high-noise regime.
Despite
the sources of noise,
we show that our dataset enables training a text-conditioned diffusion model for hand motions,
which achieves promising results across a variety of domains.
Specifically, we adapt MDM
[
81
]
to generate upper body movements,
using the SMPL-X expressive body model
[
56
]
including hand articulations.
We demonstrate encouraging performances on a manually glossed test set of BOBSL3DT, and partition
it into
seen
and
unseen
signs to assess the generalization within the same sign language BSL.
We further evaluate on a different sign language, ASL, and show superior performance of our model compared to
using the relatively small training partitions of ASL-Text and MS-ZSSLR-W.
Similar conclusion is made for the non-sign dataset of BOTH57M, depicting hand articulations as part of body motions.
Our quantitative metrics primarily measure
retrieval scores using our newly trained TMR
[
59
]
model
specialized on hand motions.
Our contributions are the following:
(i) We present a methodology to scale up the collection of motion-text pairs for describing hand and upper body motions.
(ii) Using the resulting dataset BOBSL3DT, we train HandMDM, a hand motion diffusion model conditioned on text, and obtain promising results for this relatively new task.
(iii) We conduct experiments to showcase the generalization performance of our model across several domains with increasing gap. Our code, data, and trained models will be publicly available.

]
or estimating 3D motions from videos

,

]
do not come with hand descriptions.

[

,

]
. Full-body motion capture (mocap) datasets
[

,

]
are less diverse on hand motions and smaller in size than our BOBSL3DT dataset.

descriptions from the BOTH57M dataset, which contains

descriptions are also included. Note we calculate statistics upon downloading their data, which contain slight mismatch to the original paper.
We briefly review relevant works on body and hand motion generation, as well as
sign language production.
Body motion generation from text.
Thanks to a number of text-motion datasets for full bodies, such as
KIT-ML
[
61
]
,
HumanML3D
[
26
]
,
BABEL
[
63
]
,
and Motion-X
[
38
]
,
there is a growing literature on human body motion generation conditioned
on free-form language descriptions
[
58
,
26
,
27
,
80
,
90
,
81
,
28
]
.
Variants of VAE
[
33
]
formulations were employed by initial works
that obtain promising results in this direction
[
58
,
26
]
.
The recently popularized diffusion models
[
29
]
have been adopted in later works such as MotionDiffuse
[
90
]
and MDM
[
81
]
.
Much of these works generate body skeletons and perform an optimization post-processing to produce skinned
outputs such as the SMPL body model parameters
[
43
]
.
To circumvent this costly process,
Petrovich et al.
[
60
]
incorporate SMPL representation directly in MDM training, referred to as MDM-SMPL.
In this paper, we go further by adding support for the SMPL-X
[
56
]
model, which enables hand motions.
Hand motion generation.
Works for hand generation can be grouped according to their input condition and, e.g.,
speech to gestures, object to grasps, body to hands, text to sign language translation etc.
Here, we review each category briefly.
In this paper, we particularly target conditioning
only on text description
of hands, which to the best of our knowledge is a new setting.
We differentiate our work from gesture generation given speech audio and/or body
[
53
,
64
,
5
,
25
,
65
,
86
,
94
]
, since
our goal is to generate given textual descriptions instructing how to move hands directly.
The focus of gesture generation is often to incorporate
emotions encoded in the audio
[
65
,
86
,
94
]
, or to directly infer gestures
from body motion
[
53
,
64
]
.
Another line of work considers object-centric hand motion.
Tasks include refining an initial hand-object configuration for better grasping
[
93
,
79
]
,
generating a whole-body movement to reach and grasp a given object
[
78
,
77
]
.
More related to ours, IMoS
[
24
]
generates hands given an object, its position, initial body pose, and an action expressed with text
(e.g., ‘take picture’ as text and a ‘camera’ as the object category).
Recent work shows improvements over IMoS on this text-conditioned hand-object generation task
[
14
,
13
,
45
]
.
Since these works focus on grasps, their vocabulary tends to include words such as ‘pick’, ‘grab’, ‘take’,
rather than handshape or motion as in our data.
Hand motion is often studied in isolation from bodies,
and existing datasets do not annotate descriptions
[
50
,
37
,
40
]
.
More recently, there are efforts to consider hands in conjunction with body motion.
Thanks to expressive body models that involve hand articulations,
such as SMPL-X
[
56
]
, SMPL-H
[
68
]
, Adam
[
31
]
, GHUM
[
84
]
,
whole-body datasets have been collected
[
91
,
38
]
.
However, the textual descriptions of Motion-X
[
38
]
primarily focus on bodies, and lack
significant details on hands, which are automatically annotated.
BOTH57M
[
91
]
attempts addressing this limitation by collecting
a new motion capture dataset and annotating hands, as well as bodies, with text.
But as can be seen in
Tab.
1
, the total number of motion-text pairs are much smaller
than our BOBSL3DT. Furthermore,
[
91
]
aims to generate hands
conditioned on the body movement, and not only on text.
On the other hand, the recent Nymeria
[
46
]
collection annotates hand/arm movements, but do not capture
3D fingers beyond the wrist.
Due to the inherent presence of hands in sign language (SL),
a large category of works investigate hand motion generation given
individual sign categories, or sentence translations
[
88
,
4
,
17
,
95
]
.
In the following, we provide an overview of SL generation in more detail.
Sign language generation.
Given that until recently, available SL datasets included only 2D motion modalities,
most approaches for sign language production (SLP) derive 2D body keypoints from videos using
OpenPose
[
12
]
and lift to 3D using the method proposed by
[
89
]
.
Examples include Progressive Transformers
[
71
]
,
and its followups
[
70
,
72
,
30
]
.
Several works use adversarial training to turn the keypoints into a realistic video of a signer
[
74
,
75
,
70
,
73
,
83
]
.
The work of
[
76
]
introduces an additional 3D mesh regressor to obtain the SMPL-X
[
56
]
parameters from keypoints.
A large portion of the above prior work on SLP uses the small-scale
Phoenix datasets
[
35
,
10
]
.
More recently, several efforts have been made to create larger SL datasets with 3D motion annotations.
Three concurrent works in 2024
[
4
,
17
,
88
]
have estimated 3D from signing videos
to obtain SMPL-X body model
[
56
]
reconstructions in different ways.
SignAvatars
[
88
]
adopts a combination of OSX
[
39
]
, PARE
[
34
]
, ACR
[
87
]
,
as well as a fitting step for estimating SMPL-X fits on a collection of multiple SL datasets.
NeuralSignActors
[
4
]
similarly applies fitting initialized by OSX
[
39
]
and Mediapipe
[
44
]
estimates on How2Sign videos
[
18
]
.
The very recent work SOKE
[
95
]
complements these data for CSL-Daily videos
[
92
]
, with a similar approach, also using WiLoR
[
62
]
for hand estimates.
Finally,
[
17
]
creates the ASL3DWord isolated sign dataset based on WLASL videos
[
36
]
,
leveraging the SMPL-X pose estimation model Hand4Whole
[
51
]
.
As shown in
Tab.
1
, the SL video sources for these works are much smaller than BOBSL
[
2
]
used in our work.
More importantly, they do not contain textual descriptions for hands, but only translations, mainly in the form of sentences.
Among SL datasets that contain motion descriptions, Bilge et al.
[
7
]
provide
textual descriptions for a small number of ASL signs (i.e., 250)
by manually assigning ASLLVD
[
52
]
isolated sign videos with textual descriptions from Webster American Sign Language Dictionary.
In their followup work
[
6
]
, a larger MS-ZSSLR is introduced, building on 200 sign categories from the MSASL
[
32
]
videos.
As compared in
Tab.
1
, both the number of motions and the vocabulary of descriptions are smaller than our BOBSL3DT dataset introduced
in this work.
Moreover, their primary focus is zero-shot sign language recognition using video inputs. In this paper, we extract 3D motion estimates and
use these datasets to show our model’s transfer performance.
3
Methodology
We first present our methodology to automatically scale up the
motion-text pairs using sign language data (
Sec.
3.1
).
We then describe the training of text-conditioned diffusion models
to perform hand motion generation (
Sec.
3.2
).
The overall approach is illustrated in
Fig.
2
.
Figure 2
:
Our approach:
We illustrate an overview for our data collection methodology, enabling to generate free-form textual descriptions via LLM prompting, given phonological attributes from a sign language dictionary (SignBank
[
21
]
),
as well as those detected with our HandMotionScript. The generated
hand motion descriptions are then assigned to video-based BOBSL
[
2
]
motions thanks to the automatic pseudo-glosses combined with
our THMR-based assignment.
We employ a combination of SMPLer-X
[
9
]
and HAMER
[
57
]
to extract 3D motions from SignBank and BOBSL videos.
3.1
Automatic data collection
In the following, we detail the process of collecting 3D hand motions
and generating textual descriptions for them.
We name the resulting data BOBSL3DT (videos from
BOBSL
[
2
]
, with
3D
estimates,
T
for text).
Source of video-sign pairs.
In order to collect
motion-text
pairs at scale, we resort to the
largest available
video-sign
pairs by leveraging the BOBSL dataset
[
2
]
.
The original BOBSL dataset contains 1,400 hours of continuous BSL-interpreted broadcast footage,
along with
1.2M
subtitle sentences
corresponding to the speech in the videos.
A series of works exploiting these subtitles
[
1
,
48
,
82
,
49
]
led to a strong isolated sign classifier
[
67
]
, which
employs a VideoSwin
[
42
]
architecture that
takes in a short video clip (i.e., 16 frames)
and outputs the predicted sign category within a vocabulary of 8k words.
We take these
frame-level
pseudo-glosses
(pseudo-labels) predicted
densely
in a sliding window manner
from the entire data
provided by
[
67
]
.
To reduce noise, we follow
[
67
]
by filtering low-confidence frame labels and keep sign segments with at least
[MATH: m=6]
repeated frames.
We additionally merge sign segments which are less than
[MATH: m]
frames apart.
This forms our basis for
1.9M
video-sign
pairs across the
original BOBSL
training set.
3D estimates from monocular videos.
For each signing video, we follow a series of steps to obtain 3D motion estimates with accurate hands.
We adopt the state-of-the-art 3D hand reconstruction method of HAMER
[
57
]
,
which estimates flying hands in terms of MANO
[
68
]
hand pose parameters for every video frame independently.
We observe HAMER reconstructions to provide more accurate hands than other alternatives such as SMPLer-X
[
9
]
.
Since, hand motions are characterized also by the rest of the upper body and especially arm movements,
we further apply the SMPLer-X expressive body reconstruction method, and stitch the HAMER hand estimates
onto these body estimates
with a lightweight optimization
.
We observe that while the handshapes of
HAMER are accurate, their global locations are more stable
with SMPLer-X.
We provide
more details and visual
examples in
Sec.
C.3
.
By performing monocular reconstruction on video-sign pairs from BOBSL, we obtain
motion-sign
pairs.
From signs to attributes via a linguistic dictionary & HandMotionScript.
To associate a textual label to each sign, we propose to use a linguistic dictionary.
Specifically, we employ the phonological labeling of BSL SignBank
[
21
]
,
which provides attributes about handshapes, initial/final location of each of the hands, interactions between hand and body parts,
whether a sign is one-handed or symmetric etc.
Note that these raw attributes alone do not correspond to daily vocabulary of hand motion descriptions,
but rather remain linguistic terms.
We carefully construct a pipeline to extract textual attributes from these tags
(see
Sec.
C.4
for further details).
While the SignBank attributes are accurate, they might be insufficient to describe the full sign, especially
lacking motion descriptions or remaining ambiguous for certain movements.
For example, the sign ‘SKY’ involves hands moving apart from each other; however, none of the attributes refer to this dynamic motion (they denote flat handshapes etc., see
Fig.
A.4
of the appendix).
On the other hand, some of the movements can be inferred from initial/final locations, though not precisely.
To alleviate this issue, we complement the attributes with our rule-based pose descriptions, referred to
as HandMotionScript (HMS).
In particular, we implement a method based on PoseScript
[
16
]
,
to detect frame-level features,
for the hand distances to the relevant body parts and for the palm orientations.
We use SignBank attributes to determine which body parts are relevant to measure distances.
These distances are then represented as ‘close’, ‘spread’, etc. according to thresholds,
which we adapt to our fine-grained hand motion usecase.
For example, given
a sequence of hand-to-hand distances such as [‘close’, ‘spread’],
we expect to encode the movement of ‘opening hands away from each other’.
We rely on the next step to convert these
sequence of
attributes to be interpreted as a motion.
Note that in practice, we extract
distances and orientations
along three axes separately,
which is described in
Sec.
C.5
.
From attributes to textual descriptions via an LLM.
To obtain a free-form textual description out of the above attributes, we prompt an LLM (in our case Gemini
2.5 Pro
[
23
]
)
with in-context learning. We provide few-shot examples by manually designing
six
attribute-text pairs to clearly define the task for the LLM
(see
Sec.
C.6
for the exact prompt).
With this process, we collect
sign-text
pairs for 3,259 glosses on SignBank, corresponding to 6,221 words.
As discussed in
Sec.
1
, one word may correspond to multiple glosses, due to sign variants for the same concept,
or English synonyms.
For each gloss, we ask the LLM to generate three descriptions, which allows a certain level of text augmentations.
We also generate descriptions with and without HandMotionScript, resulting in six descriptions per motion.
Those without HMS are
more hand-shape focused, while descriptions with HMS includes more dynamic information.
We note that, in our preliminary analysis, we found that existing LLMs
[
23
,
54
,
19
]
do not contain knowledge of sign descriptions
if only given the gloss information (without any attributes)
, which led to our exploration of SignBank and HandMotionScript.
Despite considerable effort, LLMs appear to only ‘know’ about a small set of ASL sign descriptions,
and remain unreliable with a fair amount of hallucinations with high confidence when it comes to
describing large-vocabulary signs or non-ASL signs. For example, prompting to describe how a certain
sign performed in BSL
may result
in description of the ASL sign.
This is why we resort to an external knowledge from a dictionary,
and also refrain from giving the gloss information in the prompt.
By going through gloss attributes instead of the gloss itself, we do not observe any concerning hallucination (see experiments in
Tab.
2
for empirical validation).
Assignment of dictionary descriptions to motions.
Once we have a collection of motion-sign pairs (from BOBSL)
and sign-text pairs (from SignBank), the next step is the assignment of textual descriptions
into motions. This is not a simple lookup as even if the pseudo-gloss points to the correct word,
we do not have the information of which gloss variant is performed, and whether that variant is present in the SignBank dictionary (see
Sec.
C.7
for examples).
To reduce the noise in this assignment process, we implement an automatic variant assignment in which
we look at the motion-to-motion similarity
between the 3D estimate on dictionary videos and each of the BOBSL motions.
At a high level, we select the dictionary motion among the gloss variants for a given BOBSL motion,
that maximizes the similarity. Note that in practice, we perform k-medoids clustering to remove motions that cannot be matched to any variant, and refer to
Sec.
C.7
for the exact details.
To measure such motion-to-motion similarity,
we train a text-to-hand-motion retrieval model,
THMR
, similar to
TMR
[
59
]
, which we describe in
Sec.
C.2
,
and use its motion encoder output as our motion embedding.
To train this model, we use random variant assignments, but observe
reliable motion-to-motion rankings since we discard the text encoder.
Our initial 1.9M video-sign pairs reduce to 1.8M
motion-text
pairs after keeping the signs that have a correspondence in SignBank vocabulary. This number further drops to 1.3M after the k-medoids assignment filtering (2,351 SignBank glosses out of the initial 3,259 are assigned to BOBSL).
Finally, we remove a portion of samples to be able to build a test set of
unseen
signs (see
Sec.
4.1
) and train our model with 1.2M motion-text pairs.
3.2
Diffusion training with SMPL-X support
Given motion-text pairs, we train a conditional diffusion model
[
29
]
to generate hand motions given text inputs.
To focus our study on the impact of automated data construction, we make minimal modifications to standard diffusion models. In particular,
we follow MDM-SMPL
[
60
]
that adapts
MDM
[
81
]
to have SMPL support.
We extend this approach to expressive upper body
by using SMPL-X
[
56
]
that encodes hands and face in addition to the body pose.
We refer to this new hand motion diffusion model as
HandMDM
.
Note that, while we incorporate face parameters in our training, we
did not find the SMPLer-X 3D reconstructions to be of sufficient quality
to capture the complexity of signers’ facial expressions, depicting mouthing words,
or other mouth gestures and facial movements. Given that our text inputs
focus on hands,
our qualitative evaluations discard faces.
We represent the SMPL-X parameters in 6D rotation, similar to
[
60
]
,
and use the parameters corresponding to the upper body.
The resulting vector is of dimensionality
[MATH: \mathbb{R}^{274}]
(i.e.,
15 6D joint rotations for each hand, 13 upper body 6D joint rotations, and 16 parameters for the face).
In terms of the architecture, we follow MDM-SMPL, which slightly differs from the original MDM
[
81
]
, i.e.,
the inputs to the Transformer encoder are (i) the CLIP text embedding token,
(ii) diffusion timestep token,
(iii) two register tokens (defined in
[
15
]
), and (iv) the noisy motion.
The model is trained to produce the denoised motion with a mean squared error loss.
During training, we sample a random text description among the multiple labels per motion.
We drop the condition 5% of the time, to use classifier-free guidance at test time.
The number of diffusion steps is 100.
See
Sec.
C.1
for further details on the guidance coefficients, number of epochs, and other optimization details.
4
Experiments
In this section, we start by describing datasets and evaluation protocols used in our experiments (
Sec.
4.1
).
We then present a series of ablation studies, such as the effect of input control, data size, and variant assignment (
Sec.
4.2
).
Next, we report results on out-of-domain datasets to test the transfer capabilities of our model (
Sec.
4.3
).
Finally, we provide qualitative analyses along with a discussion on limitations (
Sec.
4.4
).
4.1
Data and evaluation metrics
BOBSL3DT-Test.
We define a test partition of our new BOBSL3DT dataset, introduced in
Sec.
3.1
.
The work of
[
67
]
provides manual gloss annotations for a subset of
35
BOBSL test set episodes
[
2
]
spanning a vocabulary of 5.1K glosses.
Among these, we extract the signs that are present in SignBank and split them into seen and
unseen candidate signs (during training), especially to assess generalization with the latter.
We further
semi-automatically construct the corresponding text descriptions
by manually verifying the SignBank gloss variant assignments.
We refer to
Sec.
B.3
for the exact process.
Our final clean test set consists of 722 seen signs and 87 unseen signs, and includes a unique motion per sign.

:
Effect of input control:
We evaluate models trained with different input formats on the
seen
and
unseen
signs of the BOBSL3DT manually-glossed test set.
There are
722 / 87
ground-truth motion instances in these seen/unseen sets
(
with one motion instance per gloss
),
and we report the motion-to-motion retrieval from our generation to the ground truth.
Note that the first two rows use a different input at test time, strictly following the format used during training time (as opposed to the last
three
rows that are trained and tested with free-form text). For the
three
variants of LLM-generated descriptions, we test on text generated only from SignBank
phonology
attributes, as well as adding the HandMotionScript (HMS). We denote the two test set variants with a ‘
[MATH: \mid]
’ separator, i.e., ‘LLM(
Phonology
)
[MATH: \mid]
LLM(
Phonology
+HMS)’.
ASL-Text
[
7
]
and
MS-ZSSLR
[
6
]
provide
video-text pairs for ASL signs from a vocabulary of 250 and 200 words, respectively.
ASL-Text contains 1,188 training, 151 validation, and 259 test samples, with 50 unique texts in the test set.
MS-ZSSLR has 6,107 training, 1,249 validation, 1,987 test samples, with 49 unique texts in the test set.
Similarly to BOBSL3DT, we obtain the 3D motion estimates from their videos to create motion-text pairs.
We use the training sets to train
baseline models and use the test sets for zero-shot transfer from our model.
For the zero-shot case, since the test set texts include ASL-specific handshape names (28 in total), we replace these names by English text descriptions, obtained using an LLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash
[
23
]
) and manually shortening when possible.
BOTH57M
[
91
]
consists of 2,583 training, 161 validation, and 485
test motions, with their corresponding textual descriptions. However, we only use a subset of 1,483/ 101/231
train/val/test samples that have
hand
descriptions. We similarly evaluate the transfer performance on the test set, and use the training set to build the baseline.
Note that this is a motion capture dataset from 32 camera views. We only select from each pose the upper body joints used for BOBSL3DT.
We use the validation set of each dataset to tune the number of epochs for baselines.
Evaluation protocol.
Following works reporting retrieval scores for motion generation models
[
60
,
3
]
,
we primarily base our evaluations on retrieval metrics to account for the fact that there can be variance in motions corresponding to a given text.
We train a TMR
[
59
]
text-to-motion retrieval model, denoted as THMR,
with the BOBSL3DT motion-text training pairs. Unlike the initial THMR model used for variant assignment (which uses random assignments, see
Sec.
3.1
),
we retrain another THMR with the automatic assignments (
Sec.
C.2
).
For measuring performance on BOBSL3DT-Test, we report motion-to-motion retrieval scores
using THMR trained using
the same representation as our upper-body motion generations
.
Specifically, given a generated motion, we measure how often the ground-truth (GT) for the corresponding text
ranks at top-k rank (R@k).
We report both
R@1
and
R@3
.
Note that, in case of multiple GT motions per text, we mark the retrieved motion correct if the corresponding text
is
exactly
the same.
For BOTH57M, we relax this constraint given the high intra-sample text similarity,
and use text-to-text similarity as in TMR
[
59
]
to determine whether a retrieval can be considered correct (i.e., if above 0.95 in CLIP text space).
We generate motions with different random noise vectors, and report the mean and the standard variance across 4 generations.
For ASL-Text
[
7
]
, MS-ZSSLR
[
6
]
, and BOTH57M
[
91
]
,
we observe unreliable motion-to-motion similarities, explained with the domain gap (e.g., BOTH57M motions
are much longer and noisier than BOBSL3DT). In return, the generated motions can rank irrelevant GT as high, although they correspond better to the correct GT.
We therefore resort to using motion-to-text retrieval which we find to perform relatively well.
Given that THMR is trained on BOBSL3DT, we evaluate for these datasets only on a relevant subset of the features to avoid unfair comparison (see
Sec.
C.2
), namely the arm and hand rotations for ASL-Text and MS-ZSSLR, and the hand rotations for BOTH57M.
Besides the retrieval metrics, we report
FID
to measure the distance between generated and ground-truth distributions using the motion embedding space from THMR.
4.2
Ablation studies
Input control.
We experiment with a series of input formats to control the generation.
In
Tab.
2
, we report our results of training and testing on BOBSL3DT, reporting
seen and unseen partitions of the test set.
We first train a gloss-to-motion diffusion model, where we represent the gloss word
in its text form. While the performance on the seen test set is promising, this model
does not go beyond its pre-defined set of training glosses at test time; therefore, does not
generalize to unseen glosses, nor accepts free-form descriptions beyond signs.
Next, we
investigate whether the information given
to the LLM to translate attributes into free-form text can be given on its own to a motion generation model. We denote this experiment by the ‘Phonology’ row, where we train HandMDM with the text used for prompting the LLM, which contains phonological attributes detected from SignBank. While we also change the test descriptions at test time, making the rows not perfectly comparable,
we observe a drop in retrieval of the ground-truth motions
(e.g., 28.78 vs 37.53 R@3).
Besides, this model can not be applied to free-form text input, and does not easily generalize to other sign language datasets as it requires phonology attributes in SignBank format.
We now evaluate the models trained with free-form text in the bottom block of
Tab.
2
.
The ‘LLM(Gloss)’ row experiments with
generating the training text descriptions by providing the LLM with only gloss names instead of attributes.
The results confirm
that the LLM does not know BSL signs, as discussed in
Sec.
3.1
, and justifies our need for the use the SignBank attributes and HandMotionScript.
Note that the definition of ‘seen’ does not apply to this row, because we use the clean descriptions of BOBSL3DT-Test for evaluation (those generated by giving LLM the attributes).
The last two rows
of
Tab.
2
show our final models trained with attribute-based LLM descriptions.
Here, we also investigate
the gain of incorporating
HandMotionScript (HMS) in the prompt, besides the SignBank
phonology
. To obtain comparable performances, we also report on two types of test sets
that accept free-form inputs. More specifically, we analyze results
on the test set generated with
phonology
-only, and with HMS included (separated by ‘
[MATH: \mid]
’
in the table).
Unsurprisingly, training without HMS does not work well when tested with HMS (e.g.,
6.30 R@1 seen signs
), since the model is not used to the input vocabulary also including palm orientations etc.
However, the last row is more robust across test sets due to randomly sampling among text descriptions that are generated both with and without HMS,
demonstrating an overall improvement.
Training data size.
In
Fig.
3
, we analyze the impact of our large-scale training data.
We train our final HandMDM model with portions of BOBSL3DT training,
and report R@1 results on
seen and
unseen signs
with text generated from SignBank attributes and HMS
.
We observe a steady increase with more training data,
which suggests there is room for improvement with techniques for scaling up.
Figure 3
:
Training data size:
We plot R@1 performance on the
seen/unseen
test set
s
of BOBSL3DT against different proportions of the training data,
and observe a monotonic increase with larger training.

We observe gains with our automatic sign variant assignment

Sign variant assignment.
As explained in
Sec.
3.1
, we use our THMR model for performing
a text assignment in case of multiple sign variants in SignBank.
In
Tab.
3
, we measure the impact of this assignment,
by comparing to randomly assigning during HandMDM training.
We observe a considerable improvement by reducing the noise in training by this assignment step.
4.3
Transfer to other datasets
We summarize our quantitative metrics for zero-shot transfer from our BOBSL3DT-trained model
to other datasets in
Tab.
4
and
Tab.
5
.
First, we look at a domain gap between different sign languages, BSL and ASL.
The bottom block of
Tab.
4
reports two variants of our model on ASL-Text and MS-ZSSLR,
where we observe that adding HandMotionScript again leads to performance boosts
by complementing the textual descriptions with motion information.
The first block of the table shows the results of training only on ASL-Text or
only on MS-ZSSLR training sets. These baselines appear to have acceptable metrics; however,
as
can be seen qualitatively
we observe motions that have poorer fidelity
to text, while also being unrealistic
potentially due to small training size
.
We make similar conclusions on the BOTH57M dataset in
Tab.
5
,
which demonstrates a bigger domain gap from sign language motions.
Nevertheless, our model shows promising generalization capability to these
very different hand descriptions.
We note that, here, the model trained without HandMotionScript performs better, which we explain by the lack of
comprehensive motion
descriptions in BOTH57M, which tend to be more handshape focused characterized by
fingers
, not as much by
arm motion or global hand location (the purpose of HMS).
We provide qualitative comparisons to baselines in
Fig.
4
for all three datasets,
and refer to
the video on our project page
for dynamic visuals.

4.4
Qualitative analysis and limitations
In
Fig.
5
, we provide qualitative results for our model tested on unseen BOBSL3DT descriptions
(see
Fig.
A.9
of the appendix for results on the seen descriptions).
Overall, we see fidelity of our generations
whenever a handshape is mentioned in the text, e.g., fist, flat, index-middle fingers extended,
all fingers spread.
Motions such as
‘moves down towards the left hand’ (bottom right),
or ‘hands move symmetrically’ (bottom middle)
are also
visible in the video visualization of our predictions
. However, not all descriptions are
precisely
followed
(e.g.,
‘fists’ in bottom middle do not bend the fingers sufficiently
),
especially when the
handshape/
movement is fine-grained, or when the text contains too many details.
We also note a
frequent
limitation of our model, not performing contact and touch movements very precisely.
For example, the fingers are not as close to the chin in the bottom left motion.
This can be explained by the lack of precision in monocular reconstruction methods, especially
struggling with the depth dimension, leading to imperfect GT for supervision. We expect
this to be partially addressed as future reconstruction approaches improve.
An interesting avenue for future research is to explicitly detect contact
from the attributes and to enforce it in the reconstructions.
5
Conclusion
We described a methodology to scale up motion-text pairs for supervising text-conditioned 3D hand motion generation models.
The resulting BOBSL3DT dataset represents the first of its kind, providing over 1M text-motion pairs focusing on hands.
Our results demonstrate that, while noisy, LLM-generated textual descriptions guided by sign language dictionary attributes
constitute a viable alternative to manually annotating limited amount of data.
This proof of concept can be extended to other sign language dictionaries to further scale up.
We expect our model to open up a new avenue for future research in fine-grained hand movement modeling with language.

APPENDIX
This appendix provides
a brief glossary of terminology (
Appendix
A
),
an analysis of our BOBSL3DT dataset (
Appendix
B
),
implementation details (
Appendix
C
),
additional qualitative and quantitative results (
Appendix
D
).
We also provide a video on our project page to visualize dynamic motions
.
Appendix A
Glossary
We list a brief glossary to describe several sign language specific terminology used in the main paper:
[MATH: \bullet]
Gloss:
The written representation of a sign, typically a single word. In linguistic glossing, the transcription follows certain rules (e.g., adding ‘PT:’ prefix for the pointing sign ‘YOU’, assigning a unique gloss ID to each sign variant); however, in this paper, we simplify as in
[
67
]
and abuse the
gloss terminology: the sign-level annotations we use are not careful linguistic glosses, but rather free-form sign-level translations.
[MATH: \bullet]
Phonology tags:
The set of handshapes, movements, locations used to construct the signs.
See
Sec.
3.1
of the main paper and
Sec.
C.4
for the specific list of attributes included in our study.
[MATH: \bullet]
Sign variant:
One of the different ways of signing the same word.
There may be multiple ways to sign a word due to several reasons.
We give explanations and examples in
Sec.
C.7
.
Appendix B
BOBSL3DT Dataset Analysis
We analyze our large-scale BOBSL3DT dataset
by reporting several statistics (
Sec.
B.1
),
and estimating the noise level (
Sec.
B.2
).
We also provide more details about our manually cleaned test set verification
(
Sec.
B.3
).
B.1
Statistics
In
Fig.
A.1
, we plot the distribution of
word count
per unique text descriptions. We show two separate histograms for (i) the texts generated from SignBank phonology attributes and
(ii) the ones generated from SignBank attributes combined with HMS.
The difference between the mean values of the two distributions remains small (
[MATH: \mu_{\text{[Phonology]}}=40.2]
and
[MATH: \mu_{\text{[Phonology+HMS]}}=41.0]
), despite the latter containing more information.
Phonology-only descriptions close the gap by containing generic movement words such as ‘the hand moves’.
In
Fig.
A.2
, we also plot the number of motion samples per unique text description in our LLM(Phonology+HMS) training set.
Given that the glosses have a long-tailed distribution in BOBSL, the motions are not uniformly distributed across descriptions either.
The dataset includes 17,552 unique descriptions (
[MATH: x]
-axis), among which 8,201 come from Phonology-only
and 9,351 come from
the combination with HMS.
Figure A.1
:
Histograms of the number of words per text in BOBSL3DT training set:
We report the distribution of words per unique text, for the descriptions generated from SignBank phonology, and the descriptions generated from SignBank phonology combined with HMS separately.
Figure A.2
:
Number of motion samples per text description:
We observe a long-tailed distribution on the BOBSL3DT training set. The median is 33 motion samples per text.
We note two details to help interpreting these numbers.
(a) Original LLM outputs from SignBank are generated with the dominant/non-dominant hand terminology,
which are then replaced with the words right/left when assigning to BOBSL signs depending on the metadata on right-/left-handedness of signers (i.e., a left handed person’s dominant hand would be the left hand with mirrored signing).
With the original dominant terminology, we have 6,090 (Phonology) and 7,032 (Phonology+HMS) unique text descriptions on SignBank,
which then increase to the above numbers after replacing with left/right words during BOBSL assignment.
(b) The source of these descriptions are 2,351 glosses. Each gloss is converted to 3 different LLM descriptions (2,351
[MATH: \times]
3 = 7,053). Due to some glosses sharing the exact same set of attributes, we have slightly lower number of unique descriptions than 7,053 (e.g., 6,090 for Phonology portion of the dataset).
B.2
Noise estimation
We quantify the noise on a training subset of 2,525
samples by
manually checking whether the motion corresponds to the text.
We find that
61% of the motion samples correspond to their descriptions.
The main sources of noise are pseudo-glosses
(e.g., 60% of 2,624 manually-glossed test set match the pseudo-glosses),
and potentially the SignBank variant assignment.
We also note that the 3D pose estimates contribute to the level of noise,
by not strictly following the video, but our analysis here focuses on the fidelity to the text
rather than the motion realism.
B.3
Test set verification
As mentioned in
Sec.
4.1
of the main paper,
we manually verify the entire test set (seen and unseen) as follows.
We first automatically assign a SignBank variant to each BOBSL test motion, by selecting the variant with the highest cosine similarity in the THMR embedding space.
Then, for each of these SignBank samples,
we collect 4 most similar BOBSL motions,
and manually select one of them
that matches the SignBank motion, or discard the gloss if we find no match.
We also manually modified the LLM(Phonolgy+HMS) output descriptions for a subset of the test samples,
to make sure the text corresponds to the motion. Due to its smaller size, we have done this correction only on the unseen test set.
Note that the entire test set was already manually
glossed
(as opposed to the training set);
therefore, we did not need to verify the correctness of
matching between the videos and the glosses.
Appendix C
Implementation Details
We give additional information about
HandMDM training (
Sec.
C.1
),
THMR training (
Sec.
C.2
),
stitching of HAMER hands to SMPLer-X body (
Sec.
C.3
),
SignBank dictionary attributes (
Sec.
C.4
),
HandMotionScript (
Sec.
C.5
),
the LLM prompt (
Sec.
C.6
),
and
the assignment between SignBank and BOBSL (
Sec.
C.7
).
C.1
HandMDM training and inference
Similar to
[
60
]
,
we train the HandMDM networks
using a learning rate of
[MATH: {10^{-4}}]
with AdamW optimizer and a batch size of 32.
With BOBSL3DT, we train HandMDM for 300 epochs and use a guidance coefficient of
[MATH: \lambda=15]
at test time. With ASL-Text and MS-ZSSLR, we train for 2000 epochs and test with
[MATH: \lambda=5]
. With BOTH57M, we train for 300 epochs and test with
[MATH: \lambda=15]
.
C.2
THMR training
Similar to TMR for bodies
[
59
]
,
we train the THMR networks for hands
using a learning rate of
[MATH: {10^{-4}}]
with AdamW optimizer and a batch size of 32.
DistilBERT
[
69
]
text embeddings are used as input to the text encoder.
The latent dimensionality of the embedding space is 256, the temperature
[MATH: \tau=0.1]
, and the contrastive loss weight
[MATH: \lambda_{NCE}=0.1]
. The network is trained for 100 epochs.
As THMR is used for evaluation purposes,
to obtain the best possible performance, we use for supervision the 1.3M motion-text samples from our BOBSL3DT training data
prior
to filtering the unseen signs.
The input format is the same as HandMDM (see
Sec.
3.2
).
Performance of THMR on real motions.
We report THMR performances on ground truth motions in the first row of
Tab.
A.1
. Note that the unseen set is not unseen with regards to THMR
as mentioned above. We refer to
Sec.
D.1
for comments on the results.
THMR for transfer experiments.
For ASL-Text and MS-ZSSLR retrieval score evaluation, we train THMR only on the arm and hand features,
discarding the torso.
We notice that a significant portion of these datasets include seated signers, where the torso position creates a domain gap with BOBSL3DT containing standing signers. Additionally the 3D reconstruction for seated signers tend to estimate unrealistic torso bending for the ground truth, which also motivated our exclusion of the torso features.
Specifically we use the following 6D joint rotations: 2 shoulders, 2 elbows, 2 wrists and 30 for hands, resulting in a total of 216 input features.
BOTH57M full body motions are a lot more dynamic than in sign language datasets, and the textual descriptions for hands only describe finger movements (not arms). Therefore, for the evaluation on BOTH57M, we further reduce the training features of THMR to the 30 hand 6D rotations, resulting in a total of 180 features.
Figure A.3
:
Stitching HAMER hands to SMPLer-X body:
We observe qualitatively better performance
of capturing hands when using HAMER
[
57
]
, as opposed to the hand components of SMPLer-X
[
9
]
. However, HAMER only provides flying hands, which we stitch into
SMPL-X bodies estimated by SMPLer-X.
C.3
Stitching HAMER hands to SMPLer-X body
As explained in
Sec.
3.1
of the main paper,
we use a combination of HAMER
[
57
]
and SMPLer-X
[
9
]
for estimating 3D bodies
with hands from videos.
In
Fig.
A.3
, we provide SMPLer-X results
on BOBSL videos with and without using HAMER,
and observe consistently more reliable estimates with
the hand-specific and more recent approach of HAMER.
However, in terms of the global location of wrists, we find
SMPLer-X to be better since it explicitly estimates the rest of the body,
and arm movements define the hand location.
In more detail, HAMER gives us 30 hand joint rotations (local rotations
with respect to the parent in the kinematic tree), which we use
to replace those estimated by SMPLer-X.
For the wrists, we use the global wrist orientation estimated from
HAMER which are in world coordinate with the origin at the wrist.
We convert these to be local wrist orientations and replace those
estimated by SMPLer-X.
We first stitch both estimates at the wrists by using
SMPLer-X
wrist positions and HAMER wrist global orientations. This provides realistic joint positions but can lead to unrealistic wrist rotations. For instance, if SMPLer-X estimates a hand facing down but HAMER estimates a hand facing up, this first stitching results in a local rotation at the wrist of about 180 degrees, which is unrealistic.
Therefore, inspired by
[
55
]
and
[
85
]
, we then perform optimization to adjust the SMPL-X rotations of the arm joints.
We optimize the shoulders, elbows and wrists (6 rotations)
by minimizing the Euclidean distance between the 3D joints derived from the new rotations and the initial stitched pose.
Specifically, the target coordinates are the 3D coordinates of the elbows (2 joints), wrists (2 joints) and hands (30 joints). We initialize the target joint rotations with the SMPL neutral pose for each frame, i.e., with the arms positioned in a T-pose. Similar to
[
85
]
, we add a temporal smoothing term that minimizes the Euclidean distance between the joint positions from consecutive frames. A regularization term also minimizes the magnitude of the rotations to avoid unrealistic bending.
C.4
SignBank dictionary attributes
We refer to
Fig.
A.4
and
Fig.
A.5
to illustrate complete examples for the dictionary attributes.
Beyond those mentioned in
Sec.
3.1
of the main paper,
phonological information also contains whether signs are performed with only one hand, or with both hands.
In case of two-handed signs, the phonology also denotes
whether the sign is ‘symmetric’ or ‘alternating’,
and whether one of the hands is static.
There may also be information on whether forearm rotations are involved,
and whether a handshape change occurs during the motion
(in addition to the initial/final handshapes).
To transform these SignBank attributes into our LLM input, we replace linguistic terms in field names and categories with more descriptive English descriptions. Additionally, we provide several descriptions for an attribute
where possible,
as
text augmentation. We randomly select from these attribute descriptions for each gloss when inputting the attributes to the LLM. For instance, for the handshape attributes, ‘flat’ will be converted into a description among [
‘Flat’, ‘The hand is held flat with the fingers held together.’, ‘The fingers are extended and together.’
], and ‘small’ will be converted into a description among [
‘The index finger is extended and bent inward. The thumb is extended, parallel to the index finger. The other fingers are curled on the palm.’, ‘The extended index finger, bent at the palm knuckle, and extended thumb are held parallel to each other.’
]; for the tags, ‘double handed’ will be converted into the description
‘both hands are used, with the same handshape on both hands’
and ‘two handed’ into
‘both hands are used, and their motions aren’t symmetrical’
. Specifically,
we take part of the handshape descriptions
from
[
8
]
.
The full mapping can be found in our code release.
C.5
HandMotionScript
We provide
a pseudo-code in
Algorithm
1
for our HandMotionScript (HMS) pipeline,
and qualitative examples in
Fig.
A.4
and
Fig.
A.5
.
We build on PoseScript
[
16
]
designed for full human bodies. From PoseScript features, we use the hand
distances
to the relevant body parts,
determined by SignBank attributes.
If the hand location attribute is not the ‘neutral space’, but a specific body part, we compute the distances
from the hands to this body part, to detect the movement features.
If the motion is two-handed, we compute distances between the two hands. If the motion is one-handed, we compute the distances for the signer’s dominant hand only.
We further break down the distances into the
3 axes (x-y-z)
to provide more detailed information, such as left/right or above/below relationships.
As in PoseScript, we convert numerical values into text codes by assigning a range of values for each feature.
We adapt some of these ranges for our HMS pipeline.
We use the following text codes for the 4 distance features:
[MATH: \bullet]
Distance:
[
touching, close, medium, spread, wide
]
[MATH: \bullet]
x-coordinate:
[
wide/right, spread/right, medium/right, close/right, touching, close/left, medium/left, spread/left, wide/left
].
[MATH: \bullet]
y-coordinate:
[
wide/below, spread/below, medium/below, close/below, touching, close/above, medium/above, spread/above, wide/above
].
[MATH: \bullet]
z-coordinate:
[
wide/behind, spread/behind, medium/behind, close/behind, touching, close/in front, medium/in front, spread/in front, wide/in front
].
We also add a new feature to PoseScript to extract the
palm orientations
.
Specifically,
for each hand, we compute the vector normal to the wrist global orientation. If one of its global coordinate norms is greater than a chosen threshold (0.7), we assign the axis of this coordinate as the palm direction. The sign of the coordinate determines the final orientation. A palm can thus be assigned an orientation among the following possibilities, respectively to the 3 axes:
sideways, down/up, in/out
.
Once the above frame-level features are extracted, we apply the following post-processing in order to shorten them and remove possible noise. We remove every text code with less than 4 consecutive repetitions, and
we collapse consecutive repetitions into a single text code.
Furthermore, when a distance feature has multiple text codes for multiple axes, we discard the axis-dependent distance features (x/y/z) entirely to prevent too lengthy and noisy descriptions from the LLM.
Finally,
PoseScript wording uses ‘right’ and ‘left’ hands, whereas our raw SignBank descriptions follow ‘dominant’ and ‘non-dominant’ terminology (see
Sec.
B.1
).
We replace the right/left words with dominant/non-dominant according to the SignBank tags which give information on whether a signer is left-handed or right-handed.
The temporal sequence of words are then given to the LLM.

C.6
LLM prompting
We use Gemini 2.5 Pro
Thinking Experimental 01-21
[
23
]
as our LLM.
We provide
the exact prompt for generating the textual descriptions from the SignBank and HMS attributes in
Algorithms
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
and
6
.
The prompt
contains the task instructions and few-shot (
six
) examples for in-context learning.
We also include the prompt version when HMS is not used in
our project page.
We use both prompts to construct our BOBSL3DT dataset.
LLM output post-processing.
For single-handed signs, we remove any mention of the non-dominant hand ‘remaining still’ from the LLM output.
This is because in BOBSL, the non-dominant hand is rarely still (due to the natural signing speed) as opposed to the slow SignBank videos.
Furthermore, once the SignBank LLM-generated texts are assigned to BOBSL motions, we replace the words ‘dominant’ and ‘non-dominant’ with ‘left’ or ‘right’ depending on whether the signer is left-handed or right-handed using the metadata.
C.7
SignBank gloss assignment for BOBSL motions
Each BOBSL video corresponds to one pseudo-gloss, represented as a word (or more rarely a phrase).
On the other hand, SignBank is a linguistic dictionary, where each gloss corresponds to a unique
sign variant, characterized by one motion.
For example, the word ‘happy’ corresponds to three glosses HAPPY, HAPPYb, HAPPYc.
The mapping between words and glosses is complex
[
67
]
.
A word can map to multiple SignBank glosses,
and a gloss can map to multiple words.
These may be due to
multiple ways of signing the same concept,
due to homonyms (same sign motion with different meanings,
such as BSL signs for ‘battery’ and ‘uncle’),
or due to English synoyms (‘happy’ and ‘content’).
SignBank also includes
keywords
for each gloss,
related concepts which may share the same signing.
For example, the keywords for the gloss ‘HAPPY’
include ‘happiness’, ‘merry’, ‘enjoy’, ‘fun’, while
they include ‘excited’, ‘jump for joy’ for the gloss ‘HAPPYc’.
When constructing the list of
variants
for a given BOBSL pseudo-gloss word (e.g., ‘happy’),
we consider all possible keywords (e.g., ‘fun’, therefore FUN, FUNb, FUNc…),
as well as all glosses that map to this word (e.g., ‘HAPPYc’).
Once we construct a list of candidate gloss motions,
for each
sign
label in BOBSL, we perform k-medoids clustering on the set of its paired BOBSL motions combined with each candidate SignBank variant motion. We initialize the number of clusters as the number of available SignBank variants. For each cluster thus obtained, if the cluster includes: (i) a unique SignBank variant, it is assigned to each of its BOBSL samples; (ii) no SignBank variant, all of its BOBSL samples are filtered out; (iii) more than one SignBank variants, its BOBSL samples are assigned the SignBank variant that maximizes their cosine similarities.
As mentioned in
Sec.
3.1
of the main paper,
the THMR used for this assignment is trained with random assignment (since initially there is no assignment).
But since we only use its motion encoder, we do not observe a big difference
in its assignment behavior if we use the second iteration of the THMR model,
trained on these better assigned texts. This may be due to a relatively
small search space within SignBank candidates.
However, note that for our evaluations, we use the latter THMR.

For completeness, we repeat the last two rows of the
Tab.
2
of the main paper,
this time by reporting the motion-to-
text
metrics from THMR (as opposed to the
motion-to-
motion
metrics used in the main paper for BOBSL3DT).
The results in
Tab.
A.1
support our previous conclusions drawn from the comparison of motion-to-motion scores. We also complement the metrics with diversity and multimodality scores for completeness, and include ground truth evaluation as a reference (first row).
On the unseen test set, performance of the ground-truth motion to retrieve text is overall better than that of generated motions (also because the descriptions are seen by the THMR as mentioned in
Sec.
C.2
).
On the seen partition, generations outperform ground-truth motions in terms of text retrieval capability using THMR.
A potential explanation is that the generations resemble the
training
set, on which the THMR was optimized on.
This phenomenon is similar to the observations in
[
59
]
(see Table A.2 of their paper).
D.2

Tab.

evaluates the two model variants
(corresponding to the last two rows of
Tab.
2
of the main paper)
by comparing the generated motions to ground truth SignBank motions. Motion-to-motion similarity suffers from a domain gap when comparing them with the shorter and quicker signs of BOBSL. Regardless, the conclusion that using HandMotionScript
benefits still holds.
